cases.description: An empty search block means insert at the top of the file, which is unambiguous and needs no matching.
An empty replacement deletes the matched region, and the result must still validate.
Each block is located against the current content, so a later edit sees the effect of an earlier one. That matches how models reason about ordered edits.
The search block is absent, so Tier 1 fails and Tier 2 rewrites the file from the supplied replacement. Tier 2 is validated exactly like Tier 1.
A whole-file replacement that does not parse is refused. A model producing a whole file is still a model, so its output is untrusted in exactly the same way.
A replacement above the configured byte ceiling is refused with file-too-large, a distinct reason because the fix is distinct: raise the limit or use search/replace.
replacement: const b = 2; // this replacement is deliberately over the tiny limit below

cases.description: Only the whole-file tier is configured and no replacement was supplied, so the tier never really ran. tier-unavailable says exactly that rather than blaming the input.

Tier 1 refuses as ambiguous and Tier 2 has no replacement, so it would report tier-unavailable. The ambiguous diagnosis must win: it is the message the model needs in order to retry usefully, and letting a later 'the tier never ran' overwrite it destroys the only actionable feedback in the loop. The tier assertion pins the second half of the same bug — the refusal must also be attributed to the tier that diagnosed it, or every tier-1 refusal lands in the tier-2 column of the per-tier breakdown.
cases.source: packages/apply: a later tier's tier-unavailable overwrote an earlier substantive diagnosis, and the reported tier was taken from whichever tier ran last

cases.description: Tier 3 is configured but no provider exists, which is the default state: Adze must work fully without a fast-apply model, so a missing provider is reported rather than assumed.
A braces language other than TypeScript, to confirm language detection routes to the c-like validator rather than to no validator at all.
Rust, with a generic parameter list that a naive bracket counter could mishandle.
